title: Papilledema
subject: Medicine
summary: Papilledema is optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure. Recognising it guides urgent investigation for life‑threatening brain pathology, especially in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Papilledema is bilateral swelling of the optic nerve head due to impaired axoplasmic flow from elevated intracranial pressure (ICP). Diagnosis is clinical, using direct ophthalmoscopy or a portable fundus camera.
b: Bilateral disc elevation with blurred margins
Hyperemic disc, loss of physiological cup
Peripapillary hemorrhages, cotton‑wool spots

sections.p: The Frisén scale (grades 0‑5) grades disc swelling, venous engorgement and peripapillary changes; higher grades predict more sustained ICP elevation.
b: Grade 0: normal disc
Grade 1‑2: mild elevation, no hemorrhage
Grade 3‑5: marked elevation, hemorrhage, exudates

sections.p: In East African hospitals the commonest causes are infections and vascular emergencies that raise ICP.
b: Cerebral malaria or severe falciparum infection
Tuberculous meningitis
Cryptococcal meningitis (HIV)
Space‑occupying lesions (tumour, abscess)
Severe hypertensive encephalopathy
Post‑traumatic brain injury

sections.p: Patients often have headache, nausea, vomiting and visual changes; papilledema may be the first sign of raised ICP.
b: Persistent dull headache worse when lying flat
Transient visual obscurations (brief blackouts)
Bitemporal visual field loss in advanced cases

t.b: Confirms papilledema and grades severity; if unavailable, use a torch with a 90° lens and look for disc elevation
Detects mass effect, hydrocephalus, or cerebral edema when MRI unavailable
Measures opening pressure; distinguishes obstructive vs. inflammatory causes

t.a: Basic labs (CBC, malaria rapid test, HIV, TB PCR)

sections.p: Uncontrolled ICP can cause brain herniation, permanent visual loss, and death.
b: Rapidly worsening headache with vomiting
Decreased level of consciousness
New focal neurological deficit
Severe papilledema (Frisén grade ≥4)

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then lower ICP and protect vision.
b: Antimicrobial therapy for malaria, TB, cryptococcus, or bacterial meningitis
IV mannitol 20 % (if available) or hypertonic saline to reduce ICP temporarily
Elevate head of bed 30°, avoid Valsalva, give analgesia and anti‑emetics
Avoid steroids unless indicated (e.g., TB meningitis after anti‑TB drugs)
If mass lesion suspected, arrange urgent neurosurgical drainage

sections.p: Re‑examine fundus after 48‑72 h of treatment; persistent papilledema warrants repeat imaging.
b: Schedule ophthalmology review if visual loss persists
Educate patients on early reporting of headache or visual changes
Vaccinate against meningococcal disease, control malaria, ensure HIV treatment adherence

sections.p: Conditions that cause optic disc swelling without raised ICP.
b: Optic neuritis (unilateral, painful eye movement)
Ischemic optic neuropathy (disc pallor, sudden vision loss)
Papillitis (inflammation, often unilateral)

sections.p: Certain bedside tools may give false reassurance.
b: Normal CT does not exclude meningitis; CSF analysis remains essential
Optic nerve sheath diameter can be normal early in ICP rise

faq.a: True papilledema is usually bilateral; unilateral disc swelling suggests optic neuritis or ischemic optic neuropathy.

faq.q: Is papilledema always present in raised ICP?
faq.a: No; early or acute ICP rise may not yet produce disc swelling, so clinical suspicion remains vital.

faq.q: What bedside test helps when fundoscopy is unavailable?
faq.a: Optic nerve sheath ultrasound; a diameter >5 mm suggests raised ICP.

exam: A 28‑year‑old with cerebral malaria develops bilateral disc swelling – what immediate step should you take? — Verify CT is safe, then start mannitol and arrange urgent neuro‑imaging.

How does papilledema differ from optic neuritis on examination? — Papilledema is bilateral, disc hyperemic with loss of cup; optic neuritis is unilateral, painful eye movement, disc may be normal early.
What is the most likely cause of papilledema in an HIV‑positive patient with headache in Tanzania? — Cryptococcal meningitis; obtain CSF after CT, start antifungal therapy.
Why is a normal CT not sufficient to rule out a cause of papilledema? — CT may miss early meningitis or small lesions; CSF analysis is required if clinical suspicion persists.
When is lumbar puncture contraindicated in a patient with papilledema? — When imaging shows mass effect or midline shift suggesting risk of herniation.

Explain why steroids are generally avoided in papilledema unless specific indications exist. — Steroids can mask infection, raise blood glucose, and increase ICP; they are only used for TB meningitis after anti‑TB drugs.
What visual field defect is classic for chronic papilledema? — Bitemporal peripheral field loss due to optic nerve fiber compression.

How would you monitor response to treatment in a resource‑limited setting? — Repeat bedside fundoscopy or optic nerve sheath ultrasound every 48 h; clinical improvement in headache and vision also guides therapy.
